understand God’s plan and His love for us.   
Joy is not just an emotional, short-term reaction; it is an internal 
contentedness that brings a peace that few can comprehend:   
Philippians 4:7: (NASB)  And the peace of God, which surpasses all comprehension, will guard 
your hearts and minds in Christ Jesus. 
The fruit of the spirit will guard your hearts and minds.  It is the fruit of God’s 
spirit within us, and it takes work to get ourselves out of the way so that the 
fruit of God’s spirit has a place to grow. 

We are thankful to see these lessons Jesus so lovingly gave to his disciples. 
Then to have Paul write about them is such a blessing for us! 

As we move forward to the next batch of fruit, we can stand firmly and eagerly 
on the foundation of love, joy and peace. 
The next fruit of the spirit is patience.   
Didn’t Jesus tell us, “In your patience, possess ye your souls”? 

While Jesus did tell us that in Luke 21:19, it is important to realize that the 
patience or endurance Jesus spoke of there was different than the patience or 
longsuffering that Paul spoke about as a fruit of the spirit.  The patience 
referred to in the fruit of the spirit is not as commonly spoken about and has as 
much to do with restraint as it does waiting.  This is not how we normally think 
of patience. 

Patience:  Strong's Exhaustive Concordance #3115 makrothumia; (objectively) forbearance 
 or (subjectively) fortitude 
Patience:  Strong's Exhaustive Concordance #3116 makrothumos; 
 with long (enduring) temper, i.e. leniently 
Example of forbearance:  When a loan is in forbearance it means either you 
will either not have to make payments, or you can temporarily make smaller 
payments.  The loan holds back on its required payment schedule.  Taking 
advantage of this is convenient but it certainly does not help you pay back 
what you owe.  During COVID, in the United States, all student loan payments 
were suspended.  They were in forbearance. 
Patient:  Strong's Exhaustive Concordance #3114 makrothumeo; to be long-spirited, 
 i.e. (objectively) forbearing or (subjectively) patient 

Matthew 18:26: (KJV) The servant therefore fell down, and worshipped him, saying, 
Lord, have patience <3114> with me, and I will pay thee all. 
We often read this verse and think it says, “Lord, please go easy on me.” 
The word for patience here more properly means to have restraint, 
do not be angry, have forbearance.   

Why was the servant asking for this?  In those days, if you did not pay what you 
owed, you went straight to prison.  There was no negotiation, no leniency – 
straight to jail.  How someone was to pay their bills from jail is a mystery.  
Forbearance is restraint - holding back on a reaction, rather than holding up 
under difficult circumstances, which is the more common way we think of 
patience.    
Patience or longsuffering here is being defined as a willingness to be non-
reactive and appropriate.  It also tells us to be willing to wait for a situation to 
completely unfold, to be disciplined in holding back.  This patience - this 
forbearance, gives the benefit of the doubt and can only truly be displayed by 
mankind through a humble spirit. 

God’s forbearance - His patience - is our primary example:  Romans 1 was all 
about blatant idolatry and sensuality.  This is not a fun chapter to read! 
In the second chapter, Paul urges Christians to - with “long-enduring 
tempers” - refrain from judgment without proper cause and place: 
Romans 2:1-2,4: (NASB) 1Therefore you have no excuse, everyone of you who passes 
judgment, for in that which you judge another, you condemn yourself; for you who judge 
practice the same things. 2And we know that the judgment of God rightly falls upon those who 
practice such things.  
It is too easy to just judge!  Why hold back?  We have several examples of 
forbearance: 
The forbearance of God.  We are to forbear because God in His spiritual 
wisdom forbears.  If God shows restraint, we certainly need to learn this: 
4Or do you think lightly of the riches of His kindness and tolerance and patience <3115>, not 
knowing that the kindness of God leads you to repentance?  
For God’s spirit to produce peace within us, we must be 
disciplined to rise above our fleshly desires and deeds with a 
long-tempered approach, to best manage the inconsistencies we 
see before us. 
If anyone can see our inconsistencies, it is God.  He sees them in us and can 
project where they will lead us.  When we realize that God has forbearance 
with us, it is an inspiration for us to develop that kind of restraint. 
The forbearance of the prophets.  The Hebrew Christians were exhorted to 
have the forbearance of the prophets in their experiences: 
Hebrews 6:10-12: (NASB) 10For God is not unjust so as to forget your work and the love 
which you have shown toward His name, in having ministered and in still ministering to the 
saints. 11And we desire that each one of you show the same diligence so as to realize the full 
assurance of hope until the end, 12so that you will not be sluggish, but imitators of those who 
through faith and patience <3115> inherit the promises. 

Noah is a good example of forbearance.  It took 
Noah and his sons 120 years to build the ark. 
It is interesting that at the time God gave him the 
instruction to build the ark with his sons and their 
wives, he had no children!  From this, he knew it 
would be a long-term endeavor.  He was living in a 
world that had completely gone sour.  (We can feel his pain!)  We have each 
other to support us in our time, but Noah did not have anyone.  He is told by 
God he is to build this enormous, unwieldy boat which will float him, his wife, 
his sons and their wives to safety.  But he does not have any family other than 
his wife at this time.   
This is really a good example of restraint, waiting and fortitude.  Genesis 6:5 
tells us that the sin in that world had come to its full amount, with every 
inclination of the thoughts of the human heart was only evil all the time.   
It would take another 120 years for God to act on it.  We certainly see God’s 
forbearance here.   
How often did the prophets have to wait for God’s instruction when all 
seemed so chaotic? 
The prophets were always in the midst of some trouble.  God always 
came through, but in His own blessed time, in His restrained way. 
The forbearance of the teachers and pastors.  Those who are tasked with 
guiding the Christian flock are especially instructed to have forbearance: 
2 Timothy 4:1-2: (NASB) 1I solemnly charge you in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, 
who is to judge the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom: 2preach the word; 
be ready in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort, with great patience <3115> and 
instruction.  
I mentioned a few episodes ago that when I’m really focused, I am in what I 
call a “work mode.”  Recently, while swimming my laps, I was in a lap pool 
that was supposed to be for adults only.  There were kids with their parents 
playing in the middle of the lanes not moving or paying attention.  Instead of 
telling them in my usual work mode voice they should not be in the pool, I 
practiced forbearance by swimming around them time and again. 
Rick:  Jonathan, it is hard to imagine you doing this!  Your laps are important 
to you, and to be disciplined enough to swim around them (with nobody getting 
the idea that they should not be in the middle of the lap lanes!) shows a lot of 
restraint.  It was disruptive, yet you held back your anger and frustration.  This 
is a really good example for those of us that hear about this experience later. 
Our forbearance.  Our forbearance also has to do with waiting for the 
unfolding of God’s plans and prophecies.  Such waiting must be with a 
steady heart and mind:  
James 5:7-11: (NASB) 7Therefore be patient <3114>, brethren, until the coming of the 
Lord. The farmer waits for the precious produce of the soil, being patient <3114> about it, 
until it gets the early and late rains. 8You too be patient <3114>; strengthen your hearts, for 
the coming of the Lord is near. 9Do not complain, brethren, against one another, so that you 
yourselves may not be judged; behold, the judge is standing right at the door.  

The farmer had to wait for the process to be accomplished, first with the early 
rains, and second with the latter rains.  Only then could he harvest.   
The challenge came when the latter rains arrived late.  “Well, what if… 
maybe I should just…” The farmer must have restraint.  The crop is there, 
“Maybe I could harvest,”  but he was not supposed to yet. 
James is giving us a strong admonition here – to have that same 
kind of restraint.  Waiting for God’s plan to unfold can make us 
impatient with one another.  If we have this lack of forbearance 
between us, let us take it as a serious warning sign.  
Again, the prophets are an example: 
10As an example, brethren, of suffering and patience <3115>, take the prophets who spoke in 
the name of the Lord. 11We count those blessed who endured  <5278>. You have heard of the 
endurance <5281> of Job and have seen the outcome of the Lord's dealings, that the Lord is 
full of compassion and is merciful.   
Endured:  Strong's Exhaustive Concordance #5278 hypomeno to undergo, bear trials  
Endurance:  Strong's Exhaustive Concordance #5281 hypomone; constancy, patience 
Job had lost so much in his life and was miserable when covered in boils.   
His wife told him to curse God and die, but he waited patiently on the LORD.  
This is a combination of both kinds of patience.  
In Verse 10, James speaks of the brethren who have suffering and patience.  
This is the self-restraint, the forbearance we have been discussing.  Then he 
talks about the prophets who endured, the other word used for patience.  This 
is the patience we usually think of – someone who endured, who held up under 
the load.  This endurance applied to Job.  He had restraint as well.  He held up 
under the load and had restraint for his own emotions.  And we can see his 
restraint and his holding up under trial.  Both are shown, but the restraint part 
is that word patience <3115> used for the fruit of God’s spirit of patience in 
us.   
Forbearance and endurance, both parts of patience, go hand-in-hand.  All of 
our examples of patience come back to restraint.  God’s example of restraint, 
the prophets’ restraint, the restraint of those guiding the Christian flock, and 
our restraint - we need to develop restraint as a fruit of God’s spirit in us. 

As a fruit, patience (proceeding with a long temper) is far more than waiting  
for a challenge to end.  It is a developed discipline.  It is watching and waiting  
with a spiritually-based perspective and responding with a godly response.   
It is restraining our fleshly reactions and responding with grace and wisdom.   
No wonder forbearance follows peace as a fruit of the spirit! 

If we have the peace of God, it is much easier to be restrained in how we deal 
with others and with our circumstances.  We see the interconnectedness of 
what the spirit can produce in us if we are willing to allow it to happen. 
This kind of restraint gives a different meaning to patience.  Such restraint, 
along with fortitude, is necessary for all of us.  
With a healthy dose of major self-restraint in place, what is the next 
fruitage of God’s spirit in our lives? 
From love, joy, peace and forbearance the Apostle Paul next brings us to 
kindness.  When we think of something as simple as kindness, we might wonder 
why it would be listed as fruitage of God’s spirit.  As with everything else we 
have discussed, kindness certainly exists within the world.  We all likely know 
people we think are kind, so what is the difference with spiritually-driven 
kindness?  What sets it apart from the simple kindness we see around us? 
Next on the list is kindness or gentleness or graciousness (depending on the 
translation).  This aspect of the fruit is right in the middle of the list. 

Kindness:  Strong's Exhaustive Concordance  #5544; chrestotes; usefulness, 
i.e. moral excellence (in character or demeanor) 
Greek-English Lexicon: 1) moral goodness, integrity 2) benignity, kindness 
Root word of Kindness:  Strong's Exhaustive Concordance  #5543 chrestos; employed, 
i.e. (by implication) useful (in manner or morals) 
Right away we can see a difference from what we would normally expect for 
kindness.  Usefulness, moral goodness, moral excellence and integrity keep 
popping up.  The word “integrity” in the Oxford Languages Dictionary is 
defined as honest, whole and undivided.    

This is kindness with a profound depth that drives it and means much more 
than being nice.   
First, let’s realize that the only appropriate example of true moral integrity 
comes from above: 
Romans 3:9-12: (NASB) 9What then? Are we better than they? Not at all; for we have already 
charged that both Jews and Greeks are all under sin; 10as it is written, There is none righteous, 
not even one; 11There is none who understands, there is none who seeks for God; 12all have 
turned aside, together they have become useless; there is none who does good <5544> (this is 
the same word as “kindness”), there is not even one. 
Romans 3:23: (NASB) For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God. 

For God’s spirit to produce kindness or moral integrity within 
us, we must model ourselves after God and Jesus, which means 
 having a higher example than anyone or anything earthly. 
Nobody does good except God Himself and Jesus.  Jesus, as a perfect man and 
as a spirit being, did good, because he was always doing the will of God.  They 
set a very high standard.  It is a standard of integrity and moral excellence that 
does not waver.  This is what we need to aspire to by letting the fruit of God’s 
spirit grow in us.   
How do we do this? 
It takes frequent assessments of how we are 
doing.  Asking ourselves: “How am I doing in 
moral integrity?”  Is the answer:  “Well, pretty 
good.”   
That is not good enough with moral integrity.  
 Either we are on target, or we miss the mark. 
We have to let God’s spirit guide us to higher levels of moral integrity.   
To purify metals like gold, they are heated until the dross or impurities rise to 
the top.  These are dipped out, over and over, until the liquid metal is clear.  
We need to use the same method to purify our actions, frequently reassessing 
our motives and our integrity.  This is the process of getting ourselves out and 
letting God’s spirit come in. 
In Paul’s letter to Titus, he gives us a lesson in identifying the kind of moral 
integrity we should have: 
Titus 3:1-7: (NLT) 1Remind the believers to submit to the government and its officers. They 
should be obedient, always ready to do what is good. 2They must not slander anyone and must 
avoid quarreling. Instead, they should be gentle and show true humility to everyone.  
This true humility is setting the groundwork of integrity.  We cannot have godly 
integrity without true humility.  We need to have humility to invite this 
kindness into our lives.   

The attitude Paul has described is one of forbearance – having moral restraint - 
to find the good in whatever circumstance we are in.  This, in turn, opens the 
door to this level of moral excellence and goodness. 
Paul reminds us of what and where we came from: 
3Once we, too, were foolish and disobedient. We were misled and became slaves to many lusts 
and pleasures. Our lives were full of evil and envy, and we hated each other.  
He is saying:  “This is where we were.”  The Apostle Paul knew this because he 
had been there as well!  He is writing this with authority.   
As unrighteous and immoral as any of us may have been, God’s own moral 
integrity changed it: 
4But—when God our Savior revealed His kindness <5544> (moral integrity) and love, 5He saved 
us, not because of the righteous things we had done, but because of His mercy. He washed away 
our sins, giving us a new birth and new life through the holy spirit. 6He generously poured out 
the spirit upon us through Jesus Christ our savior. 7Because of His grace He declared us righteous 
and gave us confidence that we will inherit eternal life.  
See how God reveals His kindness, His moral excellence, His integrity and love 
to save us – not because we were good, but because of His mercy. 
How did God do this?   
He did it two ways: 
 Through Jesus Christ our Savior – that opened the door. 
 He generously poured out His spirit - which develops our integrity if we 
let it. 
We must realize that we can either get IN the way, stopping God’s progress in 
our life, or we can get OUT of the way so His progress can overtake our life.  
Which way should we pick?  Too often we get stuck because we do not have 
true humility. 
God’s integrity is not only a model for us now, but will shine out even more 
later: 
Ephesians 2:5-7: (NASB) 5even when we were dead in our transgressions, made us alive 
together with Christ (by grace you have been saved), 6and raised us up with Him, and seated us 
with Him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus, 7so that in the ages to come He might show the 
surpassing riches of His grace in kindness <5544> (moral integrity) toward us in Christ Jesus.  
Ages to come – this is something that is difficult to comprehend.  We live in a 
small, finite amount of time.  We live during the age of the Gospel message 
going forth, for about the last 2,000 years.  Before that was the age of Israel’s 
favor.  Prior to that was the age of the Patriarchs (Abraham, Isaac and Jacob), 
and prior to that was the time before the Flood.   

These time periods represent over 6,000 years of human history.  Over ages to 
come, thousands and thousands of years, we will see God’s kindness and 
experience, His moral excellence and integrity. 

Our moral excellence and integrity is not a stand-alone fruit of the spirit.  
• It is a developed discipline of spirituality that only comes as a result of 
God’s influence and power. 
• It needs a foundation of selfless love, which focuses us on others and not 
ourselves. 
• It needs forbearance and restraint so we can respond spiritually and not 
react in a fleshly manner.  
These are all other aspects of fruit of the spirit.  There is the spirit of 
God which produces the fruit.  It is easy to spend five episodes on 
these fruit because there is such a depth and connectedness to so 
many aspects of our characters.  For instance, kindness is not just 
simple kindness, but includes moral excellence and integrity.  It is 
life-changing!  How do we place these in the front of our lives instead 
of somewhere in the background? 
Moral excellence and integrity are necessary as we represent the 
sacredness of the gospel to all: 
2 Corinthians 6:3-10: (NASB) 3giving no cause for offense in anything, so that the ministry 
will not be discredited, 
We need to understand how big this is and be sure we do not ever discredit what 
we are tasked to represent in Christ. 
4but in everything commending ourselves as servants of God, in much endurance, in afflictions, 
in hardships, in distresses, 5in beatings, in imprisonments, in tumults, in labors, in sleeplessness, 
in hunger,  
Paul speaks of never discrediting the beauty of the gospel by our character.  
Our character has to enhance, not discredit.  Paul lists these incomprehensible 
hardships he endured that we can barely understand, but he lived through! 
Paul has just listed the hardships of his life and now lists the ways he 
conquered them: 
6in purity, in knowledge, in patience, in kindness <5544> (moral integrity), in the holy spirit, 
in genuine love, 7in the word of truth, in the power of God; by the weapons of righteousness for 
the right hand and the left,  

We have that moral integrity right in the middle of this list.  This is what Paul 
stood for.  By standing for the highest things, we do not corrupt the goodness 
of God’s plan and the gospel. 
He now lists the seeming contradictions in life.  These contradictions need 
integrity to keep them in balance: 
8by glory and dishonor, by evil report and good report; regarded as deceivers and yet true; 
9as unknown yet well-known, as dying yet behold, we live; as punished yet not put to death, 10as 
sorrowful yet always rejoicing, as poor yet making many rich, as having nothing yet possessing 
all things. 
In every one of these, Paul applies the integrity of God – taking something that 
looks bad but making it good.  That is what the fruit of God’s spirit did working 
in Paul’s life.   

As a fruit, kindness holds a deep and powerful meaning.  It is clearly based upon the 
moral excellence that came from God and was exemplified in Jesus’ daily human life.  
This level of excellence is not a human trait but is a discipline developed through 
living in selfless love and applying the previous fruit of long-tempered forbearance.  
God is glorified when we strive for such excellence! 
We never would have thought that kindness could have such a profoundly 
spiritual meaning.  This is something to strive for. 
Moral excellency and integrity pave the way for many things.  
What is the next fruit of God’s spirit? 
Living with integrity and moral excellence changes everything.  When we are 
dealing with someone who has no integrity, we have no barometer to measure 
that person’s thoughts and reactions.  This results in the reaping of doubt and 
suspicion.  However, when we are dealing with someone who has a clear 
integrity about them, we immediately reap confidence and trust.  Why?  
Because integrity provokes goodness.  This happens from the person with the 
integrity, but it frequently provokes goodness from those around that person 
because of their clear, pure example. 

Goodness:  Strong's Exhaustive Concordance  #19 agathosune; goodness, 
 i.e. virtue or beneficence 
Greek-English Lexicon: 1. uprightness of heart and life, goodness, kindness 
Good:  Strong's Exhaustive Concordance #18 agathos; a primary word; "good" 
 (in any sense, often as noun):--benefit, good(-s, things), well 
Virtue and beneficence are not possible without integrity - kindness <5544>. 
Goodness needs moral excellence and kindness.  The root word is general but is 
sometimes used with a spiritual meaning.  
God brings good: 
Romans 8:28: (NASB) And we know that God causes all things to work together for 
good <18> to those who love God, to those who are called according to His purpose. 
We are to bring good to all: 
Galatians 6:9-10: (NASB) 9Let us not lose heart in doing good, for in due time we will reap 
if we do not grow weary. 10So then, while we have opportunity, let us do good <18> to all 
people, and especially to those who are of the household of the faith. 
We know that God causes all things to work together for good to those who 
love God.  Such simplicity brings such a powerful meaning!  We also are to do 
good to all people.  Just like the word fruit, “good” is a simple word, but it 
sums up our life – this is where we are supposed to be.  We are supposed to be 
like God.  It is the fruit of His spirit growing in our lives. 
For God’s spirit to produce goodness within us, we must be in 
tune with what God through Jesus defines as goodness and 
strive to bring nothing less than His standard.  It all starts with 
selfless love. 
It always begins with selfless love because God IS love!  The fruit of the 
spirit are aspects of our heavenly Father’s character reflected in us. 

Goodness comes when we allow ourselves to be filled by God through His 
spirit with joy and peace: 
Romans 15:13-14: (NASB) 13Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy <5479> and peace 
<1515> in believing, so that you will abound in hope by the power of the holy spirit.  
Paul now adds one of the fruits that we must develop, based on joy and 
peace:  
14And concerning you, my brethren, I myself also am convinced that you yourselves are full of 
goodness <19>, filled with all knowledge and able also to admonish one another.  
On the surface it seems like this is saying: “You are such good people.  Just so 
nice!”  However, there is so much more to goodness - it is uprightness of heart 
and life.  Virtue that conforms to the standard of right.  Beneficence that is 
doing and producing good with generosity.  This is much more than just being 
nice.  It is the evidence of God’s spirit in our lives.  It pushes us to action. 
God’s goodness is a template for what true goodness stands for - it is the 
highest standard for which we can strive: 
2 Thessalonians 1:11-12: (KJV) 11Wherefore also we pray always for you, that our God 
would count you worthy of this calling, and fulfill all the good pleasure of his goodness <19>, 
and the work of faith with power: 12That the name of our Lord Jesus Christ may be glorified in 
you, and ye in him, according to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus Christ. 
God’s integrity to us is expressed by our privilege to fulfill the good pleasure of 
His goodness, of His virtue, of His beneficence, of His uprightness in heart and 
life.   
We see our part: 
Philippians 2:12-13: (NASB) 12So then, my beloved, just as you have always obeyed, not as 
in my presence only, but now much more in my absence, work out your salvation with fear and 
trembling; 13for it is God who is at work in you, both to will and to work for His good pleasure. 
God is at work in you - by giving us His spirit. 

He is giving us this part of Him so we can work His good pleasure.  As incredible 
as this may seem, it is what He gives us the opportunity to do!   
Luke 12:32: (KJV) Fear not, little flock; for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the 
kingdom.  
Who could possibly be more blessed than those given the fruit of God’s spirit to 
develop their character?  It is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the 
kingdom.  God’s goodness clearly shines in His joy over His plan for humanity.  
It is in God’s character to take more satisfaction over the giving of the gift of 
His plan than over the receiving of any gift from us. 

This is the good pleasure of our goodness: 
Ephesians 5:8-13: (NASB) 8for you were formerly darkness, but now you are light in the 
Lord; walk as children of light 9(for the fruit of the light consists in all goodness <19> and 
righteousness and truth),  
We were once in darkness, now we are children of light, and the fruit of the 
light… is goodness and righteousness and truth.   
10trying to learn what is pleasing to the Lord. 11Do not participate in the unfruitful deeds of 
darkness, but instead even expose them;  
This is why Paul gave us the two lists in Galatians 5.  He understood the human 
condition.  This shows us how God's character is its remedy, and we must apply 
His spirit and allow it to grow in us.   
12for it is disgraceful even to speak of the things which are done by them in secret. 13But all 
things become visible when they are exposed by the light, for everything that becomes visible 
is light.  
We have to stay sound and clear and focused on goodness. 
To develop the discipline of a life lived in spiritual goodness: 

 Realize that you are now a child of light 
 Know what God expects of those who are children of 
light 
 Expose darkness through God’s light 
It is appropriate to discuss the contrast of light with dark deeds along with the 
fruit of goodness.  Goodness is the application of integrity and is about being a 
child of light.  We are not children of light because we, of ourselves, are so 
good or virtuous with a nice character.  It is because we are dwelling in the 
righteousness Jesus bought for us and have God’s spirit working within us. 
Romans 2:6-7: (NASB) 6(God)…will render to each person according to his deeds: 7to those 
who by perseverance in doing good <18> seek for glory and honor and immortality, eternal life;  
What does doing good bring?  Glory and honor and immortality.  There is no 
better gift offered to any being, human or spirit!  There is no higher plane of 
existence.  God’s character has to be able to shine through us.  Our goodness is 
an important reflection of Him. 

As a fruit of the spirit, goodness stands upon the development of 
the long temper of patience and growing the moral excellence of 
kindness.  This virtue, this uprightness of heart and life, is the 
outward expression of forbearance and integrity.  It cannot exist 
without patience and kindness.  All three of these fruits could not 
be functional without selfless love as a foundation.  We are tasked 
with learning and applying patience, kindness and goodness 
from the inside out.  That is what Jesus did. 

We keep going back to the character of God, and we should.  The life of Jesus 
was built around accomplishing the will of God.  Therefore, he was the shining 
example of the character of God.  Goodness is right in the middle of all of this! 
Galatians 5:22-23: (NASB) 22But the fruit of the spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, 
kindness, goodness, faithfulness, 23gentleness, self-control; against such things there is no law.  

In the Episode 1258, the final one in this series, we examine faithfulness, 
gentleness and self-control.  They are the final result of selfless love...and a 
maturing Christian life.  

While these three pieces will complete the Apostle Paul’s list, they also 
represent the beginning of our journey to a fuller Christian life! 
This episode has been about patience, kindness and goodness - understanding 
self-restraint and moral excellency, as well as the virtue that stands on moral 
excellency is the character of God.  Christians have the opportunity to let 
God’s character shine through our lives.  What are we doing about that? 

So, do I walk in the spirit of the lusts of my human nature?

How Is Satan Trying to Devour Me? 

1 Peter 5:8: (NASB) Be of sober spirit, be on the alert.  
Your adversary, the devil, prowls around like a roaring lion,  
seeking someone to devour. 
Most Christians are very aware of Satan’s influence in our world 
today.  We know he is opposed to God and His will at all turns, 
and as the god of this world (2 Corinthians 4:4), he will 
ferociously fight to keep all that he has laid claim to.  What we 
do not often think about is how we, as individual Christians, fit 
into the intensity of Satan’s raging against God.  The Scriptures 
tell us that his objective was and continues to be to usurp the 
authority for himself that ultimately belongs to the Most High 
God.  Anyone and anything that in any way, shape or form 
stands in the way of Satan’s fight over his perceived authority 
is fair game for his unrighteous anger.  As Christians, we love God supremely and 
seek to daily walk in the footsteps of our Lord Christ Jesus.  This blessing means 
we are also Satan’s prime targets.  What now? 
The Apostle Peter sets the stage for the dramatic battle Satan wages upon 
the followers of Jesus: 
1 Peter 5:6-11: (NASB) 6Therefore humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that 
He may exalt you at the proper time, 7casting all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you. 
8Be of sober spirit, be on the alert. Your adversary, the devil, prowls around like a roaring lion, 
seeking someone to devour. 9But resist him, firm in your faith, knowing that the same 
experiences of suffering are being accomplished by your brethren who are in the world. 10After 
you have suffered for a little while, the God of all grace, who called you to His eternal glory in 
Christ, will Himself perfect, confirm, strengthen and establish you. 11To Him be dominion 
forever and ever. Amen. 
We will refer to 1 Peter 5:6-11 throughout this entire podcast and unfold this 
battle against the roar of Satan.   
(Source:  https://wildexplained.com/why-do-lions-roar/)  Roaring and making sounds are a 
vital part of lions’ interaction with each other and other animals.  A lion’s roar can be heard up 
to 5 miles away.  They use different types of roars to communicate different things.  While a 
fierce roar is a warning sign to intruders, they are using other types of sounds with their pride 
members….  Do lions roar when hunting?  We have seen in the movies that lions roar when 
hunting.  Like many things in Hollywood, this is just dramatization and has no connection with 
real life.  Lions do not roar when hunting. 
(Source:  https://www.scienceabc.com/nature/secret-behind-lions-roar.html) 
Male lions roar for various reasons - a lion may roar to scare off an intruder, another lion or a 
 predator.  It could also roar to warn its pride of imminent danger. 
If lions do not roar when hunting, what does it mean that like a roaring lion, 
the devil is seeking someone to devour? 
Devour:  Strong's Exhaustive Concordance #2666 katapino; to drink down, 
 i.e., gulp entire (literally or figuratively) 
 The King James Version translates this word as devour, drown, swallow (up) 

Here are two examples of where this same word is used:  
Matthew 23:24: (KJV) Ye blind guides (Jesus was speaking to the Pharisees), which strain at 
a gnat, and swallow <2666> a camel. 
1 Corinthians 15:54: (KJV) So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this 
mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, 
Death is swallowed up <2666> in victory. 
Seeking someone to devour is not looking for a meal to eat; rather, it is seeking 
to completely consume or obliterate someone or something.   
If Satan is not hungry, why does he fiercely roar at us?   
Because we follow Jesus, who came to take the kingdoms of the world from 
Satan: 
Luke 4:5-8: (NASB) 5And he led him up and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a 
moment of time. 6And the devil said to him, I will give you all this domain and its glory; for it 
has been handed over to me, and I give it to whomever I wish. 7Therefore if you worship before 
me, it shall all be yours. 8Jesus answered him, It is written, you shall worship the Lord your God 
and serve Him only. 
Here is the line in the sand:  Jesus will only worship his heavenly Father!   
Satan pronounced the world belonging to him.  He sees us as predators and 
intruders on his territory, as we serve the Lion that is from the tribe of Judah.  
Jesus is identified as that Lion:  
Revelation 5:5: (NASB) and one of the elders said to me, Stop weeping; behold, the Lion 
that is from the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has overcome so as to open the book and its 
seven seals. 
It is not about a meal.  For Satan, it is about dominion or protecting his domain 
from Jesus who has overcome and is coming to remove the kingdoms of this 
world from him.   
A lion’s roar is said to be as loud as 114 decibels, which is the equivalent to 25 gas-powered 
lawn mowers.  At 120 decibels, hearing damage can potentially occur. 
Satan’s roar is saying:  GET OFF MY TURF OR YOU WILL REGRET IT – YOU ARE IN 
MY WAY! 
The lion’s roar is big, powerful and scary!  Going beyond hunger, Satan as a lion 
is protecting what he perceives to be his.   
(Source:  https://wildexplained.com/why-do-lions-roar/)  Regarding hunting techniques: 
The primary way is by stalking its prey.  Lionesses would stay hidden for as long as possible and 
then approach the target.  When they get close enough, they would charge and chase the prey.  
The secondary tactic is reserved for hunting larger prey.  The pride would corner the animal 
 and come at it from different sides.  In this scenario, male lions also join the hunt. 
While the lionesses do most of the hunting, when there is a larger target, the 
entire pride is gathered to destroy the prey.  It is interesting that a group of 
lions is called a “pride.”  Satan’s “pride” is very powerful.  When lions in a 
pride hunt together, they are formidable and dangerous. 

These scriptures describe Satan’s pride – his army: 
Ephesians 6:10-12: (NASB) 10Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of His might. 
11Put on the full armor of God, so that you will be able to stand firm against the schemes of the 
devil. 12For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the 
powers, against the world forces of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in 
the heavenly places.  
Satan’s pride consists of those under his control.  Our struggle is against the 
rulers (plural), …powers, …world forces, …spiritual forces, …in the heavenly 
places – all plural.  This describes Satan’s army that is ready, willing and able 
to surround anyone crossing the line onto his turf.   
As Christians, we are targets.  We need to pay close attention to Peter’s words 
about how Satan prowls around like a roaring lion.   

For Satan to neutralize us, he is going to disrupt the path we are walking.   
His object is to destroy our heavenly victory.  He wants us out of the way at 
any cost.   
Being a follower of Christ is to be living our lives in the middle of a spiritual 
rebellion with Jesus at our side. 
The powerful, paralyzing and fear-invoking roar of Satan 
 comes to us in many ways.  How do we prepare?  

Staring down this battleground we find ourselves on can be daunting, to say the 
least.  It is so important to remember we are standing where we stand because 
God through Jesus has arranged it so.  Our Father knows we can be victorious 
as long as we are spiritually armed and ready to stand for truth! 
Our theme text gives us four ways to internally prepare for the lion’s roar 
and his attack: 
1 Peter 5:6-8: (NASB) 6Therefore humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that He 
may exalt you at the proper time, 7casting all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you. 
8Be of sober spirit, be on the alert. Your adversary, the devil, prowls around like a roaring lion, 
seeking someone to devour. 

INTERNAL PREPARATIONS     
We are warned that the lion will roar, but God tells us how to counteract the 
attack.  As a soldier of Christ, we learn to be armed for battle on the inside, 
not just the outside. 
These four ways to stand against Satan’s intimidation can and should be 
personal for each of us.  In the last segment, we touched on wearing the whole 
armor of God.  

Think about the armor protecting us from the outside in:  
Ephesians 6:13: (NASB) Therefore, take up the full armor of God, so that you will be able 
to resist in the evil day, and having done everything, to stand firm.  
Interestingly, it does not say to take up only the sword, or the shield, or the 
breastplate of righteousness, but the full armor of God, so that we can stand 
firm. 
Wearing this armor enables us to stand and fight the godly battles before us.   
If we ever try to fight those battles without God’s armor, we are doomed.  We 
have to be armed from the outside in. 
In addition, we need to be sure we stand and fight for what is holy: 
1 Peter 1:14-15: (NASB) 14As obedient children, do not be conformed to the former lusts 
which were yours in your ignorance, 15but like the Holy One who called you, be holy yourselves 
also in all your behavior; 
If we are sanctified with God’s spirit within us, we are supposed to be holy, set 
apart for God’s purposes.  This means wherever we go and whatever we do, the 
fully-armed Christian solider is walking on holy ground.   
On Episode 1220: “Can Faith Take Me From Failure to Victory?” we went over 
the account of Joshua getting ready to battle for the city of Jericho.  This was 
the first city to conquer as they entered the Promised Land.  An angel of the 
Lord came down to talk to Joshua and told him to remove his sandals because 
he stood on holy ground.  Where God’s influence is, the ground is holy.   

Joshua was standing just outside the walls of the pagan city of Jericho, but 
because God’s angel was there, that ground was holy.  Therefore, wherever we 
go with God’s spirit and when we are doing God’s work, that ground is also 
holy.  This is why Satan wants us out of the way so badly - we bring holy ground 
wherever we go!   

Think about the four preparedness steps as protecting us from the inside out.  
When applied, they validate us as “armored up” soldiers of Christ. 
1 Peter 5:6: (NASB) …Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God…  
Satan sometimes aims his roar at a central source of our human need 
for security. 
This source of our security can be things like strong and reliable friendships, 
our home or anything that gives us a sense of security.  Sometimes in our 
experiences that source of security is protected, and we merely suffer 
temporary inconvenience.  That source is challenged and it hurts, but we can 
get through it.  But sometimes that source of security is damaged or even 
destroyed, leaving us feeling vulnerable.    
Am I humbly keeping all of my true security in God through Christ? 
When a soldier is unsteady and insecure in his or her position, they become 
weak and easier to overtake.  When we do not feel secure and circumstances 
go beyond what we perceive as our ability to cope, we get anxious and 
depressed. In such a state we are easier to overtake.  The question is, am I 
going to fall apart when something or someone I depend on goes away? 
I was really shook up at the beginning of the pandemic when no 
one really knew what was happening or even how COVID-19 was 
transmitted.  I love food and am sad to admit that I have taken 
food security for granted.  When I saw empty shelves at my 
grocery store after waiting an hour to get in, I broke down and 
cried out of fear and disbelief.  This was new to me.  I felt like 
grabbing the animals and hopping into the Ark!  I don’t take this for granted 
anymore.  My prayer now is:  “Thank you, LORD, for all the times I had food 
available at the speed of thought.”  I have to ask myself, how will I react if this 
becomes a regular occurrence like it is now in many parts of the world?   
Looking at Julie’s experience, we can see her sense of food security was put 
under trial – Satan ROARED at her over this just like he roars at any of us when 
what makes us feel secure is challenged.     

Would we desert the Lord because we cannot find our next meal? 

1 Peter 5:6: (NASB) Therefore humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that He  
may exalt you at the proper time. 

It is easy to take our earthly sources of security for granted.  Satan knows this 
and the ferocity of his roar can sometimes be focused on redirecting all our 
attention towards the preservation or replacement of that security.  Our fear 
of loss is now positioned to compromise our spiritual security.  We panic and 
try to get our security back.   
When our security is challenged or damaged, are we humble enough to look at 
this experience as within the realm of God’s providence so that we can keep 
moving forward?  Or, does the regaining of that security become the only 
important thing in our life?  Can we only hear his roar (fear caused by the loss 
of our security) drowning out what else we are supposed to be doing?  Satan’s 
roar is there to intimidate us.   

Even doing the mundane things of life can be holy work.  Going to work and 
stocking shelves can be holy work.  It is a place and a way to let our light shine.  
As we go about our daily lives, we must maintain the focus that we are about 
God’s holy work and not get overrun by the fear of losing our security. 
Whether we have lost a source of our human security or not, how do we 
step back and view our circumstances? 
Philippians 3:8: (NASB) More than that, I count all things to be loss in view of the surpassing 
value of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord, for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and count 
them but rubbish so that I may gain Christ. 

The Apostle Paul was an accomplished Pharisee.  He was well-known, well-
educated, intelligent, aggressive, disciplined and passionate.  He knew the 
word of God.  He had all of this going for him.  Remember, as he was on his 
way to destroy Christians, he was stopped by Jesus and called to become his 
follower.   

Once Paul came to Christ, he looked at all of his amazing accomplishments as 
but rubbish – it was all garbage - so that I may gain Christ.   
He still had to make a living, so instead of a lofty teaching job as a Pharisee, 
he preached the gospel and supported himself as a tentmaker.  This was holy 
work.  Everything from the past was trash.  If we want a good example of 
someone whose security was interrupted, we need only look at the Apostle Paul 
on the road to Damascus.  Talk about ripping the security out from under 
someone with a complete life interruption!   
In contrast to the ferocity of Satan’s roar of threat and destruction, let’s go 
 back to Jesus, the Lion of the tribe of Judah. 
Here is his invitation to his followers: 
Matthew 11:29: (NASB) Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and 
humble in heart… 
While Satan roars to intimidate us regarding our earthly security, here we see 
in contrast how Jesus calls us to work alongside him in the holy work he himself 
was called to do.  What a privilege! 
Notice the gentleness, the care with which Jesus calls us - Satan is a roaring 
lion seeking to devour and Jesus is the Lion from the tribe of Judah, the 
rightful king.  Jesus says, Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am 
gentle and humble in heart… we can trust in that.  Can we trust in Satan?  Not 
even close!  Jesus is meek and humble in his lion-like authority, a completely 
different picture than we have from Satan.  
When it comes to our sources of security, we have choices to make between 
humbly accepting God’s providence in our lives or listening to Satan’s roar. 
We love all those people and things that make us feel secure, and yet we need 
to see them as God would have us see them. 

We know Satan goes after what gives us security. 
How much further is he willing to go to beat us down?   

Because this is a desperate spiritual battle being fought by Satan, we can 
unfortunately be assured that he will not stop at anything in his attempts to 
usurp God’s authority.  We need to understand that his highest value targets at 
this end of the age are those who have God’s spirit and do God’s will. 
There is a battle and the assurance that if we are a Christian walking in the 
footsteps of Jesus, we WILL be attacked.  We WILL be intimidated.  Satan WILL 
seek to not only knock us off the path, but to put us out of commission 
wherever possible.   

1 Peter 5:7: (NASB) Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you. 
Satan sometimes aims his roar at our hearts – our very core.   
Our hearts carry the deepest of all our human attachments.  These can include 
parents, children, spouses, extended family and our most powerful friendships.  
Sometimes things - serious things - happen to them.  Sometimes we get through 
such things, and sometimes our hearts are crushed by unfathomable tragedy.  
Either way, the question remains:   
Am I holding my own anxiety or am I whole-heartedly handing it over 
to God through Christ? 
Sometimes we suffer traumatic loss 
through death, divorce, betrayal and 
sickness.  This causes massive anxiety.  Do we maintain ownership of our 
anxiety because that is the way humans are built?  

If I look at my anxiety like a piece of property, who holds the 
deed?  Do I own the deed to my anxiety in my own name, or 
have I signed it over to the LORD through Jesus?   

To “cast” does not mean to just casually lay it down.  It means to throw it 
away from you. 

When casting a fishing line, you throw it out and you miss…you reel it 
back in, then you throw it out there again…wrong spot again; it takes 
all this work – then finally!  It lands in the right spot…YES!  The pressure 
is off and you finally have peace.  
Casting all your anxiety on Him is easy to say when it is not our spouse 
who is dying.  We are not walking hundreds of miles with a suitcase and 
a baby trying to cross a border to get to safety.  Casting anxiety are 
just words.  How do we make them real?   
Here is help to link us to that reality: 
1 Peter 5:9: (NASB) But resist <436> him, firm in your faith, knowing that the same 
experiences of suffering are being accomplished by your brethren who are in the world. 
Resist:  Strong's Exhaustive Concordance #436 anthistemi; to stand against i.e., oppose 
Satan’s roar is a ferocious challenge and warning to those who follow the Lion 
of the tribe of Judah to leave Satan’s territory or else be overwhelmed or 
consumed.  Coping with the loss or tragedies of our loved ones can be 
debilitating, time consuming and discouraging.  During such time, it is a great 
comfort to realize that our brotherhood is also standing, fighting and 
overcoming the ferocity of Satan’s roar!  It can be done. 
The Apostle Peter understood this in a profound way.  When he describes the 
roar of Satan coming to devour, destroy and obliterate us, he adds into the 
context the encouragement to resist – stand against - because the ground on 
which we stand is holy.  We know the same experiences which we have are 
being accomplished by your brethren, wherever they may be.   
How do we make those experiences real?  Engage in the experiences of the 
brotherhood - fellowship, communicate and feel what they are going through 
while sharing what we are going through.  Mutually bear each other’s burdens, 
protect each other, walk together.   
We may not be the one walking hundreds of miles with just a suitcase like so 
many are now with the war in Ukraine, but we can put ourselves in a position 
where we can be supportive.  We may not be able to feel it like they are 
feeling it, but we can be a part of their experience and they can be a part of 
ours.  The apostle is telling us we need each other.  It is not a one-on-one 
battle.  It is not just 
Rick in his armor, 
standing there facing 
Satan.  It is Rick 
standing with 
Jonathan on his right 
side, Julie on his 
left, and all the 
other brotherhood 
surrounding him so 
that we can all stand 
together.     

One of my Christian friends recently lost her husband to an 
unexpected heart attack in his sleep.  She and their 16-year-old 
son are devastated.  Everyone reacts in different ways – some 
might curse God and run away from their faith, but she is trusting 
the LORD will care for them and has redoubled her efforts to 
study and be close with our church group.  They are still deeply  
                   grieving.  We do not want to minimize in any way the grieving  
                   process.   
Standing your ground does not mean forgetting the grief and being tough or 
moving on immediately.  No, standing your ground is to experience appropriate 
grief.  It does hurt – we need to work through all of the stages of grief.  These 
are needed and valuable for our mental health.  Grief can be a growing 
experience, especially if we go through the process knowing the providence of 
God is guiding us.  Then we can grow through that grief.  Standing your ground 
means going through that grief and handing it over to God, giving it into His 
hands when the time is right.   

In contrast, rather than ferocious threats, let’s look at the approach of 
Jesus to all of humanity: 
Matthew 11:28: (NASB) Come to me, all who are weary and heavy-laden, and I will give you 
rest. 
If you are resting, you are not anxious.  If you are anxious, you are not resting. 

Many times when I am finished with a project and supposed to 
rest, I am rest-less.  If I am restless, it means I am anxious and 
have not let go enough.  This is a challenge for me. 

While Satan may roar at us over the deepest matters of our hearts, Jesus 
beckons us to come to him for rest from the deepest matters of our hearts.  
Satan wants to derail us using these deep matters of our hearts.  Jesus wants to 
give us rest so he can get us through these experiences. 
We could have called this episode, “How to Not Fall Apart When Things Go 
Really Wrong.”  A lot of that is doing what we are doing here – preparing, 
steadying ourselves, learning and breathing deeply in between the difficulties.  
This reminds us of the word “resilience.”    

A soldier on the outside looks pretty strong, all armed and ready to go.  But 
what does that soldier look like on the inside?  Here is where the roar of Satan 
will get to us.  We can have our armor on but will still shake when we hear that 
roar.  Are we prepared on the inside to manage that roar?   

Resist.  Be more prayerful every time Satan is more active.  He will soon give it up, if he finds that 
his attacks drive you to Christ.  Often has Satan been nothing but a big black dog to drive Christ’s 
sheep nearer to the Master. – 19th century English preacher C.H. Spurgeon 
Am I allowing Satan’s roar to push me away, to derail me?  Or, am I using the 
roar to get closer to the Father?  It is His providence which will guide and 
protect me because I have His armor on the outside, and I am casting my 
anxiety on Him on the inside. 
Imagine the lion roaring at us, lined up together as soldiers with our armor on.  
The reason we can be successful is because we are standing on holy ground 
with the giant Lion of the tribe of Judah standing behind us!  If God is for us, 
who is against us? (Romans 8:31) 

                            (Editor’s Note: This has been corrected from the audio) 

Now for our third way to internally prepare for Satan’s attack: 
1 Peter 5:8: (NASB) Be of sober spirit…   
Satan sometimes aims his roar at the sources of our personal 
stability.   
This roar can be particularly frightening, as our ability to be firmly established 
to care for ourselves is usually at the heart of our ability to serve God.  
Sometimes we have protections that can keep us going or ways to temporarily 
plug our stability holes.  But other times we may end up losing everything as a 
result.   

Am I with a sober spirit facing the disruptive and financial challenges 
before me, knowing that the very hairs of my head are all numbered?  
Examples of this might be losing our job, not having a retirement pension, our 
alimony ends - how will we make ends meet?  Financial uncertainty is 
consistently ranked as one of the top stressors in the United States.  
According to Thayer's Greek-English Lexicon, to be of 
sober spirit is to be “calm and collected in spirit, to 
be temperate, dispassionate and circumspect.”  It means we need a clear 
direction for our focus. Through all of these trials and scary challenges and 
heartaches, we cannot lose sight of our true direction in life. 
If we put down our spiritual armor, we become too vulnerable to Satan’s 
attacks and he wins. 
I think of this like we have to be “spiritual Weebles.”  
Weebles were a little egg-shaped toy I played with as a 
child.  They were designed in such a way using a weight 
and gravity that they couldn’t tip over or stay on their 
side – they would always right themselves.  The slogan 
was “Weebles wobble, but they don’t fall down.”   
We might wobble in any one direction for a time, but 
want to right ourselves back to the center of our 
personal stability.  Be the Weeble!   

It is God’s providence and direction – and sometimes redirection - that brings 
 the challenge to the faithful followers of Jesus.  Satan will try to misdirect us. 
In contrast, rather than ferocious threats, let’s look at how Jesus calms our 
lives: 
Matthew 11:29: (NASB) Take my yoke upon you and learn from me… and you will find rest 
for your souls. 
While Satan roars to instill serious doubt when the personal stability of our 
lives is either threatened or interrupted, Jesus promises that working alongside 
him will give rest to our souls.   

Be determined - not distracted - even though we feel that roar all throughout 
our being.  Satan’s attacks on our lives can be deeply personal.  Always be 
awake, aware and wearing the armor of God! 
Satan attacks our personal security,  
our very hearts and our personal stability.  What is left? 

This conversation is to focus us on the fact that when trials happen in our lives, 
we can be sure of two things:   
1) Satan will inevitably attack to try to thoroughly intimidate us and 
shake our faith.   
2) Most importantly, we can be sure of God’s care and guidance to get 
us through these experiences!   
Satan attacks – God cares.  God’s providence is more powerful than Satan’s 
attacks as long as we stay with God’s providence.   

We cannot let this subtle detail change us.  We must STAND DEVOUT in faith.  

The fourth way to prepare internally for the lion’s roar: 
1 Peter 5:8: (NASB) …be on the alert...   

Satan sometimes aims his roar at our physical beings.  
This roar can be upsetting on the deepest of levels as it can cause us to see 
how fragile and terminal our lives can be.  When looking at my life through the 
eyes of it ending, the capacity for regret, insecurity and fear can dramatically 
escalate, all of which creates greater liability to be devoured by the adversary. 
To hear more on how to be strong 
during difficulty, listen to our 
friend Vicki’s courageous battle 
with cancer on this episode: 

Two months ago, unbeknownst to me, I had several blood clots 
form in my legs and travel to my lungs.  They were accumulating 
there while I thought I had other issues, since other health issues 
were going on.  On the January 24, 2022 episode, I could barely 
string two sentences together without getting out of breath.  
My wife was aware that something was wrong.  She complained to 
our daughter, an Advanced Practice Registered Nurse (APRN), who made me 
check my blood oxygen.  My blood oxygen level dropped through the floor while 
exercising, and I was in the emergency room the next morning.  Several doctors 
told me very plainly that our daughter saved my life.  Apparently, one lung was 
pretty much not working and the other was on its way out.  They said I was in 
line to just drop dead because the clots were accumulating uninhibited.  This 
caused me to stop and reconsider everything about my Christianity - things that 
had been done, things that had not been done.  Asking the Lord, if it is my 
time, please take care of my beloved wife and family.  Satan tried, but God’s 
providence was bigger.  By God’s grace, I lived to breathe another day.   
We have to look at these experiences and realize that while Satan’s roar tried 
to get me at every turn, God’s providence provided a very attentive wife and a 
 very alert daughter to literally give me a second chance. 
Sometimes we have cures and treatments that can bring us back to health and 
full energy.  Other times, these issues can lead to years of pain and suffering, 
 and even the end of our Christian walk.  
Physical pain, especially when it is long-term, is a very difficult trial.  When we 
are in pain, we can think of little else other than trying to get relief.  We have 
to really redouble our efforts to remember that we cannot be both resentful 
and grateful at the same time.  We have to consciously choose gratitude - 
sometimes it is a moment-by-moment choice. 
Some preachers of the so-called Prosperity Gospel say that we can pray for 
healing and if we are a good Christian, only positive things will happen to us.   

Do Rick’s blood clots mean he sinned somewhere along the line and was being 
punished?  According to Hebrews 5:8, Jesus learned obedience from the things 
which he suffered.  Why would we expect any less?  This is how we learn heart 
reliance on God.  It is not about being punished as much as it is about being 
taught.  Our experiences teach us and often alert us to a better path on which 
to travel. 
I looked at that experience as the providence of God.  I needed a 
“wake-up” call, so by God’s grace, He gave it to me.  He literally 
allowed me to wake up and continue to live another day to work 
further in His service.  Trials and difficulties are supposed to 
happen.  Just understand that when we suffer, the roar is loudest. 
Am I with an alert heart and mind facing my physical issues knowing 
that God’s grace and blessing will never leave me as long as I 
persevere? 
To be on the alert is to be vigilant, meaning to be awake and 
giving strict attention. This implies that we remain focused on 
the most important thing (which is our call to sacrifice and 
follow in the footsteps of Jesus) while handling all our earthly responsibilities.  
How many times have we driven some place where we have 
gone regularly?  We find ourselves on autopilot, not 
remembering how we got there.  Then suddenly a bicyclist 
jumps out and we were shook up because we were not expecting it.  We need 
to be constantly on the alert, expecting that dangerous lion to be lurking 
around the corner waiting to devour us.  We cannot go through our Christian 
lives on autopilot because Satan’s roar will devour.  Instead, we need to stand 
in a devout way! 

In contrast, rather than ferocious threats, let’s look at how Jesus 
encourages our sacrificial lives: 
Matthew 11:30: (NASB) For my yoke is easy and my burden is light. 

What an incredible difference between the attempts to obliterate us versus the 
soft-spoken power and might of the Lord Jesus, the Lion of the tribe of Judah.  
While Satan’s roars can amplify our physical challenges, the message of Jesus is 
simply that he will never leave us or forsake us.  His yoke FITS my life.  His 
burden is not heavy; it is blessed!  This is what we need to remember when the 
roar of the lion comes to shake us up so that we can be devoured.  Stand your 
ground! 

It is all in the hands of God, but Satan is allowed to attempt intimidation, fear, 
derailment, second-guessing, anxiety, depression and more.   
But God’s providence is still always there.   
In conclusion, RESIST Satan’s roar.  All of us as a body must work together 
to resist his roar: 
1 Peter 5:10-11: (NASB) 10After you have suffered for a little while,  
 After you have withstood the roars of the adversary… 
After you have held each other up and served our Lord Jesus and each other in 
this most holy work of our lives… 
the God of all grace, who called you to His eternal glory in Christ,  
The Almighty Father who created this magnificent plan of salvation and invited 
you to it… 
will Himself perfect, confirm, strengthen and establish you. 11To Him be dominion forever and 
ever. Amen. 
The lion’s roar IS all about dominion!  The Apostle Peter, as he finishes this 
letter, reminds us that it is, was and ever will be about God’s dominion.  
Let that lion roar; WE STAND OUR GROUND!  
He is going to roar – Satan is desperate!  We are armed on the outside and need 
to be armed on the inside in order to withstand the roar.  The roar is not a 
physical roar; it is a mental and emotional battle.   
Who wins?  We live at the end of the age, and we know the world is crumbling.  
This is a life and death battle.  
The Apostle Paul subtly and eloquently lets us know how this battle will 
turn out: 
Romans 16:20: (NASB) The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace 
of our Lord Jesus be with you. 

When we look at the picture of the body of Christ, the “feet members” are the 
final part of the body.  There is no more body after the feet.  It is an 
illustration for the end of the age.  Satan will be crushed because God will put 
him under our feet.  The Father puts his soldiers in the right place at the right 
time.  As soldiers, how can we help?  By remaining faithful to the things that 
we know and are called to do.  We need the external armor and the internal 
preparedness to make sure the armor is used appropriately.     
• Satan sometimes aims his roar  
          at a central source of our human needs and security. 
• Satan sometimes aims his roar  
         at our hearts – our very core. 
• Satan sometimes aims his roar  
         at the sources of our personal stability. 
• Satan sometimes aims his roar  
         at our physical beings. 
What will we do when these attacks happen?   
God’s providence is a conquering power as we stand against the roar 
of the lion: 
Romans 8:35-39: (NASB) 35Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will tribulation, or 
distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword? 36Just as it is written, for 
your sake we are being put to death all day long; we were considered as sheep to be slaughtered. 
37But in all these things we overwhelmingly conquer through Him who loved us. 38For I am 
convinced that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor 
things to come, nor powers, 39nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing, will be able 
to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.  
These scriptures sum up the battle we have been talking about.  God’s 
providence is ever-present in the lives of true Christians.  Satan’s roar is also 
ever-present.  His objective:  To devour, to obliterate, to knock us out and 
take us away from our mission to serve our LORD God Almighty.  Make the 
choice to stand armed on the outside and armed on the inside!   
True Christians follow Jesus because he came to take the government of this 
world back from Satan.  As individuals, we are helping to accomplish the will of 
God through Christ.
